Putting parameter-free pooling in place of a convolution on the direct input->output edge loses capacity (exp 20, -7 to -14).
Adding a conv where the direct input->output edge was empty creates a new learnable path to the output (exp 11 fits).
If edge 3 is already empty, removing edge 4 leaves the output depending on edge 5 alone (exp 4, IN16 -16.9).
Deleting a 3x3 conv into the output should cost more than deleting a skip, which can sometimes help (exp 1).
Replacing a 3x3 conv into the output with pooling removes the cell's main learnable path (by the general conv-vs-pool pattern; untested here).
With edge 2 empty, node 2 is fed only by edge 1, so making that edge a pool degrades the whole node-2 branch (exp 13 fits).
Adding a conv where the node1->node2 edge was empty adds depth and capacity, which should help more than swapping out an existing op (untested here).
When edge 4 is empty, the direct edge carries more of the output, so making it a strong conv should matter more (untested here).
Replacing a 3x3 conv into the output with a parameter-free skip loses capacity, whereas filling an empty edge 4 does not (untested here).

raw:
Hypotheses rest on two patterns in the 20 experiments and in what is generally known about NAS-Bench-201:

- **Output paths are fragile.** Node 3 is the sum of edges 3, 4 and 5. An edit that removes or degrades the only strong path into node 3 hurts badly (exp 4, 15). An edit that restores such a path helps a lot (exp 16).
- **Op-for-op swaps.** Replacing a convolution with pooling, or with skip/none, usually costs accuracy (exp 3, 20). Adding a convolution where there was `none` or pooling usually helps (exp 11, 18).

The "why" lines below call an experiment "in favour" when it fits the hypothesis. That is not a measured interaction: a single experiment only shows the edit's effect under one parent, and none of the 20 compares the same edit with and without the condition. So these are untested; hypotheses 6, 8, 9 and 10 have no direct experimental support at all.
